newsitem.title: USA: Specialty coffee meeting to focus on supply of quality beans.
newsitem.headline: Specialty coffee meeting to focus on supply of quality beans.

text.p: As some 8,000 participants in the coffee trade -- from producers to retailers -- meet at the Speciality Coffee Association's 9th Annual Conference & Exhibition this weekend, one of the most pressing issues they face is how to ensure there will be enough high-quality coffees to supply this fast-growing industry.

The number of outlets selling premium coffee beans in the United States has soared from about 200 in 1989 to more than 5,000, the SCAA estimated. In 1999, they expect gourmet outlets to double to 10,000, with sales of $6 billion.

As the speciality market has grown -- and more American consumers have become accustomed to the taste of better quality coffees -- large roasters such as Folgers and Maxwell House have flocked to the gourmet sector.

Analysts say the increased demand for quality arabica beans has contributed to the tight supply in the United States, where concerns about low inventory levels pushed coffee prices last week on New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange to $2.18 a pound -- the highest price in more than 2-1/2 years.

"Behind the shortage of coffee is the growth of the speciality market," said Ted Lingle, the executive director of SCAA. "There's no question that supplies of fresh mild coffees, the kinds used in the speciality industry, are in tight supply."
To boost supplies of quality beans, coffee farmers should be well compensated for their crops, which would encourage them to increase production, he said.
"Our view is: prices are too low," said Lingle. "We want to increase and maintain some stability at high price levels so we can maintain supply."

Consumers, he said, should be educated so that they understand why certain coffees are more expensive. One way to to help differentiate beans is to set up an appellation system similar to the one used by grape farmers in the wine industry.
Appellation tied to origin would not only designate quality, but enhance marketing by promoting the unique quality of coffee grown in a specific region.
Lingle would also like to see another pricing mechanism developed, where roasters and growers can deal directly with each other.

"We're trying to find a method that achieves better balance between supply and demand without a widely fluctuating price," he said. "We don't want to change the futures market, but what's missing today is a system for the top end where coffees are traded by specific lots and roasters have the opportunity to sample the coffee."
"The SCAA started out by wanting to change the industry. This forum is the opportunity to make changes."
